opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think it's one of the more genuinely exciting directions in robotics right now, though I'd put some caveats around it.

The core insight is really nice. Classical motion planning, things like RRT or trajectory optimization, works well when you have a clean model of the world and a well-defined cost function. But a lot of real manipulation tasks are messy. There are many valid ways to do them, and the distribution of good actions is multimodal. If you train a standard regression policy on human demonstrations, and half the demos go left around an obstacle and half go right, you get a policy that averages them and drives straight into the obstacle. Diffusion models handle that multimodality naturally. They learn the whole distribution and then sample one coherent mode. That's a big part of why things like diffusion policy suddenly made imitation learning feel a lot more reliable.

The second thing I like is that you're generating a whole chunk of trajectory at once instead of a single action per timestep. That gives you smoother, more temporally consistent behavior, and it makes it easier to add constraints or guidance at sampling time, like steering away from collisions or toward a goal, without retraining.

The caveats are mostly practical. Inference cost is real. Iterative denoising is slow compared with a single forward pass, and robots need to react quickly. A lot of work goes into distillation, fewer sampling steps, or flow-matching variants to get the latency down. Then there's generalization. These models are only as good as the demonstration data, and collecting high-quality robot data is still the bottleneck. Diffusion doesn't magically solve out-of-distribution situations. And you still want some safety layer or classical check underneath, because a sampled trajectory that looks plausible isn't guaranteed to be feasible.

So my overall take is that it's a real step forward in how we represent robot behavior, especially for dexterous, contact-rich tasks where hand-engineering costs is hopeless. But I see it as one piece of the stack, probably combined with larger pretrained models that provide higher-level understanding and with classical methods that provide guarantees. The exciting future is the hybrid, not diffusion replacing everything.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think diffusion for planning is one of those ideas that's genuinely exciting but also easy to overhype, and I say that as someone who spent years working on robots before I came to Anthropic.

The core insight is really appealing. Classical motion planning, sampling-based stuff like RRT or trajectory optimization, treats every problem as a fresh search. You have an objective, you have constraints, and you grind until you find a feasible path. It works, but it's slow, it's brittle to how you set up the cost function, and it has no memory. Every time the robot picks up a mug it's solving the problem from scratch.

Diffusion flips that. You learn a distribution over trajectories from demonstrations, and then at inference you sample from that distribution, and the beautiful part is that the denoising process is naturally multimodal. If there are two reasonable ways to reach around an obstacle, a regression model will average them and give you a path that goes straight through the obstacle. A diffusion model will commit to one or the other. That alone solves a problem that bit us constantly with earlier behavior cloning approaches.

The other thing I really like is that you can inject constraints during sampling. You can do guidance toward a goal or away from a collision without retraining. So you get this hybrid where the learned prior gives you plausible, human-like motion, and classical constraint satisfaction nudges it toward correctness.

Where I'm more skeptical is on three fronts. First, latency. Running dozens of denoising steps for every plan is expensive, and robots care about tens of milliseconds, not seconds. There's been good work on distillation and consistency models that collapse that, but it's still a real engineering tax. Second, out-of-distribution behavior. These models are only as good as the demonstrations, and the failure modes are confident and smooth-looking rather than obviously wrong, which is actually worse for a safety-critical system. A planner that fails loudly is easier to wrap in a safety layer than one that fails gracefully into a wall. And third, I think people underestimate how much of the hard part in robotics is still perception and contact, not the kinematic path. Diffusion gives you a nicer trajectory. It doesn't tell you the object is slipping.

So my overall read is that it's a genuine step forward, especially for manipulation where demonstrations are abundant and the multimodality really matters. I'd expect it to become a standard component in the stack. But I'd frame it as a very good learned prior that still needs the classical machinery around it, rather than a replacement for planning. The teams that get the most out of it will be the ones that treat it that way.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s promising, particularly because robotics often has many valid ways to solve the same problem. If you’re reaching around an obstacle, you might go left or right. You don’t want to average those two trajectories and drive straight into it. A diffusion model gives you a way to represent those different possibilities and generate a candidate trajectory.

The question is how you turn that candidate into something you can reliably execute. Does it respect the robot’s dynamics? Is it collision-free? Can you generate it fast enough to replan when the world changes? A trajectory that looks plausible isn’t necessarily a safe plan.

So I’m excited about using it as part of a system: learn a good distribution of possible motions, then use constraints, verification, and feedback to make those motions work on the actual robot. The test is whether it makes the robot more successful in unfamiliar situations, within the compute and latency budget you actually have.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s promising, especially because robotics is so multimodal. If you’re reaching around an obstacle, you can go to the left or to the right, but averaging those two good trajectories gives you a bad trajectory straight through the obstacle. Diffusion gives you a way to represent those different possibilities and sample a coherent motion.

The question is how you turn that into something you can execute reliably. A trajectory can look plausible and still violate a collision constraint or be dynamically infeasible. And if you need many denoising steps before you can act, latency becomes a problem, particularly when the environment is changing.

So I’m excited about using it to propose trajectories, combined with constraints, verification, and feedback from a controller. The important test is whether it makes the robot more successful at the task, including when something unexpected happens.
